title: The Lord of Powers and the Gates
english: Taking these things up, they speak to the heavenly powers, to those dividing the heavenly gates. Then they inquire, 'Who is this King of Glory, whom you announce is coming, to whom the gates must be lifted and the eternal ones—not the temporary ones—the immortal ones, must be raised up?' Near to this is what is brought forward in Isaiah: 'Who is this coming from Edom, with garments stained red from Bozrah? Why are your garments red?' (Isa 63:1). And they inquire again.

Even if this body, being raised from the dead, and especially the one of the Savior previously, does not possess the characteristics of flesh having been transformed into spiritual, yet by the grace of the one ascending, traces were preserved for the recognition of where the one ascending comes from. And because of this: 'Garments stained red from Bozrah' (Isa 63:1). And just as having risen from the dead and appearing to the disciples, desiring to confirm to them that the body which he had has risen, he showed the marks of the wounds, he showed the side, not that the body possesses a side—for to bear a side is hard and prototypical—but so that he might be fully known as the one who rose, so that they might not think badly concerning the resurrection from the sign of the fullness of the resurrection, as if after the resurrection the raised body carries the characteristics of the corruptible, 'he entered through closed doors' (Luke 24:40); so also here, being taken up, immediately after the ascension, he showed the characteristics of the flesh, not so that they might remain; nor did those things which he showed, such as having eaten and the marks of the wounds and the others, remain with him having them. Not so that we might eat, for he ate after the resurrection, but so that they might see that he, whom he said, was himself the one who rose. This indeed Luke says: 'To whom he also proved himself alive after his suffering, by showing many proofs and by eating and touching' (Luke 24:39-43). Observe that he also proved himself alive after his suffering by eating.

Lift up your heads, O gates, and be lifted up, O ancient gates, and the King of Glory shall enter (Ps 24:7). Who is this King of Glory? They inquire: concerning whom is this said that he shall enter, so that we may open the doors for him and lift them up? He says: 'The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in war' (Ps 24:8). He makes the answer from His works. As at the beginning of the ascent to...

The mountain of the Lord: 'and who shall stand' (Ps 24:7). And 'how many' was not used—not that Abraham or John [were meant]—but 'if anyone is innocent in hands and pure in heart', so also here he did not say 'how many', but by deed he showed the matter: 'the Lord is mighty and strong, the Lord is strong in war' (Ps 24:7, 8). As it began, these things were pre-proclaimed. But when he rose and was ascended, it is no longer said that 'he will come out' (Ps 24:8), the one who transformed the kingdom upon the earth, the one who destroyed the power of death, the devil; but he is 'mighty and strong, the Lord is strong in war' (Ps 24:8). Comparing that prophecy which has it thus: 'the Lord of powers will come out and will crush the war'. As it began, these things were pre-proclaimed. But when he rose and was ascended, it is no longer said that 'he will come out' another 'the Lord is strong in war' having brought down the tyrants.

The Lord is strong in war: 'lift up your gates, O rulers of you' (Ps 24:7). Since they asked who it is, and having said it, they asked 'which are the gates' and to open [them], they say: since the Lord is mighty and strong and strong also in war, do not hesitate, do not delay. And behold: to those in charge he says: 'lift up the gates' (Ps 24:7). And since the gates also are rational, and toward them he stretches out, saying: 'and be lifted up, eternal gates' (Ps 24:9). And 'be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will come in' (Ps 24:10). Therefore he says: 'the Lord of powers, this is the King of glory'.

Often the armies are signified by the name of power. The Lord is of these powers, of the heavenly armies; for such powers appeared to the shepherds praising God when Christ was born. And altogether the Lord is of all these powers, of the thousands and myriads praising and ministering. And it is possible to take the powers thus: each rational substance acting as a power of holiness. Just as we say a musical woman and a grammatical woman, when she possesses these things, so the one participating in 'Christ, the power of God' (1 Cor 1:24), each is a power. Therefore, the Lord is of these powers. But the power is to be understood in two ways: either each rational substance participating in the power of him, the Savior, is called a power, or the army of the rational substances, the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Soul and the Flesh; Davidic Authorship
english: Thus they are arrayed for battle. Who is this king of glory? The Lord of powers, He is this king of glory. Do not seek who He is regarding what we say; for the Lord of powers, He is. And you also are powers, and each of you a power according to the second meaning. 'Lord' therefore; because with authority He said that 'He is the king of glory.'

Concerning this power and this manifestation, Paul also writes: 'The mystery of godliness is great, for He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit' (1 Tim 3:16), and 'taken up in glory' (Acts 1:11). The one taken up in glory is the Lord of glory, He is the king of glory.

It is not to receive now a word ill-interpreted in an unseasonable way by some. They wish to say that 'the Lord of glory, having been crucified' is the God Word; for those denying the perfect humanity say that 'the one crucified, the Lord of glory' is the same God Word. And such is indeed the syllogism which those who err thus say, and the reasoning of Apollinaris the heretic, who says that 'the Word' became 'flesh' by a change of essence, and such syllogisms which Apollinaris set forth in his writings: Christ was crucified. The one crucified is the king of glory. Therefore, Christ is the king of glory.

And thus they hear the syllogism: 'Christ is the king of glory. Christ was crucified. Therefore, the king of glory was crucified.' And these people speak monstrosities. The cross is manifest; for it is a fixing down of a body; 'they pierced my hands and my feet' (Ps 22:16). He who says that the God Word was incorporeal being crucified allegorizes the cross. And when the cross is allegorized, the resurrection will also be allegorized. And when the resurrection is allegorized, all things that happened are as if they were dreams.

And these people say the same things; for even if they name [it] for the sake of some deception: body and body? And if you say 'yes', that very body is not other than the God Word. So they are two. So are we not saying two? For what is absurd, to say two, the temple and the one in the temple? For the body is called the temple of the Savior. And it is not said: 'who was manifested as flesh', but 'in flesh'. And again: 'having been put to death in the flesh'. It has not said: 'having been put to death as flesh'. 'Every spirit that confesses in the flesh' (1 John 4:2)...

and having come. Therefore, even if they do not wish, there are two: the flesh and the one seen in it. But we do not call the flesh without soul; for this flesh, having been produced, has become without soul, as it is evident to us. 'The flesh dwells in hope, because you will not abandon my soul to Hades' (Ps 24:14). If it had remained in Hades, the flesh would not have had the hope of resurrection. But previously they inquired: 'Who is this king of glory?' (Ps 24:8) and they heard an answer; then, since the king of glory is not a random person, they inquired with greater precision and a second time, and moreover they received another answer, no longer 'the Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord is mighty in war' (Ps 24:8); for perhaps it was possible to suppose that one of the powers had been chosen by God; and he says: 'The Lord of powers, he is the king' (Ps 24:10). Thus I call him the Lord of powers, not as a power.

A Psalm of David. The psalm is said to be 'to David'; for it is one thing to be 'of David' and another to be 'to David'. 'Of David' is said when he himself has composed or is singing. But 'to him' is said when it is brought to him. If, therefore, I say that this triumphal hymn is to the athlete, to the victor, then David has set a subscript. And the things said do not stand only regarding his own person, but also if another should be found according to him. Who then is this David? 'Who will do,' he says, 'all my will' (Ps 40:8). Let the psalm be said concerning everyone who does the will of God.

'To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul' (Ps 25:1). It is not for everyone to say: 'To you I have lifted up my soul, O God.' But he who is able to say: 'My soul lives to him' alone lifts up his soul to God. God is in highness; I do not speak according to a place—and often these things have been made clear to us—but in a highness of surpassing nothingness. When someone therefore tears away from the things below his own soul, from the devil and the causes of evil and of evil itself, he lifts it up to God, so that it may live to him alone, so that it may dwell with him, so that 'having been joined as one spirit' it may become to him. It is a great thing to say this voice, having an unknowable soul. 'If our heart does not condemn' (1 John 3:21), he says, 'we have boldness toward God.' When the heart is known, being checked by conscience, [it is not...]

title: Shame and Hidden Sins
english: One is able to say such things about oneself. But such a person is rare, and because of the difficulty of finding them, they are perhaps thought by some not to exist at all. Furthermore, the rarity is shown by the proverbist saying: 'Who shall boast having a pure heart and shall speak boldly as being free from sin?' (Psalm 25:3). By saying pure, he means the heart being rightly disposed and thinking concerning piety. He who is persuaded according to the truth, that one has a pure heart. And he who is outside of practical sin speaks boldly as being free from sin.

Because the truth and those things thought truly purify the soul and the heart, Peter the apostle writes: 'having purified your souls in the obedience of the truth' (1 Peter 1:22). And James writes: 'Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, double-minded' (James 4:8). They cleanse hands, those making their actions crooked, and they purify their soul, those casting away all double-mindedness; 'and purify' indeed, he says, 'hearts, double-minded.' Most of all, those thinking wrongly are double-minded. Sometimes they are seized by glory and held by it, but when they look at things otherwise, they find them to be having [something else], and how they once remain in the grasping bad-glory.

Thus, one is presented as free from sin who has lived a life according to the right way. He has a pure heart, the one thinking the things of the truth, having taken 'the mysteries of the kingdom' (Matthew 13:11) in soul and having been initiated according to them. This one, therefore, lifts up the soul toward the Lord. It is not one who happens to do so who lifts [it]. To say [it] is perhaps easy for everyone, but to do [it] is either difficult or has reached the point of being nearly impossible, not because of his own nature.

And this, since according to the apostle 'no one says Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit' (1 Corinthians 12:3). And these men themselves, when they call the God Lord, do not say [it] with voice alone, but with deed and disposition. When they act thus, disposed as toward a master, doing what he wills and commands, they are truly slaves; and since what is turned toward [him] is that of a truly slave, he is truly a master. 'My God, in you I have trusted; let me not be put to shame' (Psalm 25:2). Happy is the one having precise knowledge, having trusted in it, who converses with all and is not put to shame. He who has trusted in virtue is not [cut off]...

They act wickedly; therefore, they are not ashamed. For those committing sin are the ones undergoing shame. Some say, 'they shall rise up for reproach and eternal shame.' Thus the word prays for the unfeeling that shame may come to be for them: 'fill their faces with dishonor'—speaking regarding faults—'and let them be ashamed and perish and know that you are the Lord' (Ps 51:1-4). When they feel [shame], being such wicked people, they perish according to that state in which they are.

The one who is confident in his iniquities, if he knows that he sins wickedly, is ashamed and perishes as a wicked man, not as a rational substance. Because of this the apostles say: 'we have spoken the hidden things of shame' (2 Cor 12:7). We have not spoken only the manifest things producing reproach and shame, but also the hidden things. And it can be so: for some, the things of drunkenness are hidden. When they are intoxicated in wines, such as they were regarding whom Paul writes, 'whose glory is in their shame' (1 Cor 5:31), in whom it is necessary to be ashamed, they themselves wish to be honored. Indeed, one finds fifty men wishing to be honored through much variety.

But how are they hidden? I have spoken of the hidden things in two ways: sins are in thoughts. Therefore, not only does the diligent and the simple man refrain from practical deeds, but also from the hidden things, as he also sends up a prayer: 'cleanse me from my secret [sins]' (Ps 51:3). Otherwise, the unknown things are called hidden. Having been bold regarding all manifest transgressions, that they are forgiven him, the saint says: 'who will understand transgressions?' (Ps 19:12). He who understands transgressions is rare.

Since it is possible for me to be ignorant of them, 'cleanse me from these. Spare your servant from others' (Ps 51:3)—for they are foreign to me, to my essence, both they and those acting them against me. And furthermore he adds: 'lest they overpower me.' If the hidden things do not overpower me, 'then I shall be blameless.' And he adds: 'and I shall be cleansed from great sin.' We say these things are in thoughts, and to be so as to be unknown to the possessor. How then is the one being cleansed from these 'from great sin' cleansed? You know that the 'great' of [it] is in relation to what. As for the one desiring to be entirely pure, even the small things of sins seem to be great. And they once took such a pattern: if a garment many times...
